interactions.label: Which source accounts for the largest volume of haemorrhage in pelvic fractures?

params.question: Which source accounts for the largest volume of haemorrhage in pelvic fractures?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The superior gluteal artery is the most commonly injured artery in pelvic fractures and bleeds fast, but arterial bleeding contributes less total volume than venous bleeding. Arterial injury is best managed by angioembolisation.

answers.text: Low-pressure bleeding from the presacral venous plexus and pelvic sidewall veins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The presacral venous plexus and sidewall veins produce high-volume, low-pressure bleeding that accounts for the majority of pelvic haemorrhage. This is why pelvic compression with a binder is so effective — it reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous bleeding.

answers.text: Cancellous bone surface bleeding from the fracture site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone surfaces do bleed continuously in pelvic fractures, but this contributes the smallest volume of the three sources. It is difficult to control directly and usually stops once the fracture is stabilised.

answers.text: Direct injury to the common iliac artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Common iliac artery injury is rare in pelvic fractures. The most frequently injured artery is the superior gluteal artery, a branch of the internal iliac. Even so, arterial bleeding is not the predominant source by volume.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three sources of pelvic haemorrhage: venous (presacral plexus — largest volume), arterial (superior gluteal — fastest flow), and bone surface (continuous but smallest). This distinction guides whether you use a binder, angioembolisation, or packing.
Well done. Understanding that venous bleeding predominates explains why pelvic compression and volume reduction — rather than immediate surgery — are the first-line haemorrhage control measures.

interactions.label: A patient with a spinal cord injury who has preserved perianal sensation at S4–S

params.question: A patient with a spinal cord injury who has preserved perianal sensation at S4–S5 but no motor function below the injury level is classified as having a complete spinal cord injury on the ASIA scale.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Any preserved sacral function at S4–S5 — including perianal sensation alone — means the injury is incomplete (ASIA B or higher), not complete (ASIA A). This single finding changes the prognosis dramatically, which is why meticulous testing of S4–S5 must never be skipped.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is an incomplete injury. Sacral sparing, defined as any preserved function at S4–S5 (perianal sensation, voluntary anal contraction, or toe flexion), reclassifies an injury from ASIA A (complete) to ASIA B or higher (incomplete). This distinction is critical because incomplete injuries carry a dramatically better prognosis for neurological recovery.

params.question: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. She is hypotensive with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture. At which anatomical level should the pelvic binder be applied?

answers.text: At the level of the iliac crests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the most common error. Placing the binder at the iliac crests applies force above the widest point of displacement and fails to reduce pelvic volume adequately to tamponade venous bleeding.

answers.text: At the level of the anterior superior iliac spines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ASIS is too high for effective pelvic compression. The binder must sit lower, at the greater trochanters, to counteract the outward rotation seen in open-book injuries and reduce the volume where bleeding accumulates.

answers.text: At the level of the greater trochanters

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The pelvic binder is applied at the level of the greater trochanters. At this level, it compresses the pelvis at its widest displaced point, effectively reducing pelvic volume and tamponading venous haemorrhage. This is especially effective for anteroposterior compression (open-book) injuries.

answers.text: At the level of the pubic symphysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pubic symphysis is too low and anterior. Placing a binder here would not encircle the pelvis effectively and would fail to apply the circumferential compression needed to reduce pelvic volume.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pelvic binder must be placed at the greater trochanters — not the iliac crests, which is the most common error. At the trochanters, circumferential compression reduces pelvic volume, tamponading the venous bleeding that causes most pelvic haemorrhage.

Excellent. Correct binder placement at the greater trochanters is a life-saving skill. Remember that the binder works by reducing pelvic volume to tamponade venous bleeding, and is most effective for open-book (APC) injuries.

interactions.label: Why do open pelvic fractures carry a mortality rate of 30–50 per cent, significa

params.question: Why do open pelvic fractures carry a mortality rate of 30–50 per cent, significantly higher than closed pelvic fractures?

answers.text: Open fractures always involve more complex fracture patterns with greater bony displacement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While open pelvic fractures are often severe, fracture complexity alone does not explain the mortality gap. A closed fracture with equally complex displacement would have a lower mortality because it lacks the contamination risk.

answers.text: Massive haemorrhage is compounded by faecal or urinary contamination, leading to pelvic sepsis and multiorgan failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The lethal combination in open pelvic fractures is haemorrhage plus contamination. When the fracture communicates with the perineum, vagina, or rectum, bacteria enter the pelvic space and can rapidly progress to pelvic sepsis and multiorgan failure.

answers.text: The pelvic binder is contraindicated in open fractures, removing the primary haemorrhage control tool

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A pelvic binder can still be applied in open pelvic fractures as a temporising measure. The high mortality stems from the combination of bleeding and wound contamination, not from an inability to use a binder.

answers.text: Nerve injuries from posterior ring disruption cause neurogenic shock that compounds the haemorrhagic shock

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While nerve injuries from posterior ring disruption do occur and affect bowel, bladder, and sexual function, they do not cause neurogenic shock in this context. The high mortality is driven by haemorrhage combined with wound contamination leading to sepsis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The high mortality in open pelvic fractures is driven by massive haemorrhage combined with faecal or urinary contamination through the wound. This leads to pelvic sepsis and multiorgan failure, which is why early recognition and multidisciplinary management are critical.

Well done. Recognising the haemorrhage-plus-contamination pathway is essential. As a house officer, your most important role is early recognition — checking for perineal wounds, vaginal or rectal lacerations, and open skin defects communicating with the fracture.

params.question: A patient with a suspected pelvic fracture has a negative FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) scan. Why does this NOT exclude significant pelvic haemorrhage?

answers.text: FAST technology cannot detect blood flowing at low pressure from venous sources

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: FAST can detect free fluid regardless of whether it came from arterial or venous sources. The limitation is not about blood-flow pressure but about where the blood collects — FAST looks for intraperitoneal fluid, not retroperitoneal.

answers.text: Pelvic haemorrhage is primarily retroperitoneal, which FAST does not visualise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid. However, most pelvic fracture haemorrhage collects in the retroperitoneal space, which FAST cannot assess. A patient can lose several litres of blood into this space with a completely negative FAST scan. CT with contrast is needed to evaluate retroperitoneal bleeding.

answers.text: The pelvic binder compresses the abdomen and creates acoustic artefacts on ultrasound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a binder may slightly affect image quality, this is not why FAST misses pelvic haemorrhage. The fundamental limitation is anatomical — FAST assesses the peritoneal cavity, but pelvic bleeding accumulates in the retroperitoneal space.

answers.text: FAST has poor sensitivity in the first hour after injury before sufficient blood has accumulated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While FAST sensitivity does improve with larger volumes of free fluid, timing is not the key issue in pelvic fractures. Even hours after injury with litres of blood loss, FAST may remain negative because the bleeding is retroperitoneal, outside the area FAST assesses.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is anatomical: FAST detects free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, but pelvic fracture haemorrhage is primarily retroperitoneal. A negative FAST does not exclude life-threatening pelvic bleeding. CT with contrast is required to evaluate the retroperitoneal space.

Excellent. This is a critical pitfall: never be falsely reassured by a negative FAST in a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture. The retroperitoneal space can accommodate massive blood loss without producing intraperitoneal free fluid.
